category: Programming: functions, control flow & error handling
description: Writing MATLAB programs: defining functions and validating their inputs, the control flow keywords, error raising and catching, function handles and the functional-programming helpers, variable scope, and the dynamic evaluation functions.

tools.name: function
tools.description: Declares a function, giving it a name, input arguments and output arguments, and opening a new scope whose variables are private. A file may contain a main function followed by local functions visible only within that file, and functions can also be nested or defined at the end of a script. Functions are the primary unit of reuse and the only way to get well-defined inputs and outputs.

parameters.name: out1, out2
parameters.description: Output arguments; assign them in the body before returning.

parameters.name: in1, in2
parameters.description: Input arguments, passed by value semantically.

tools.notes: MATLAB uses copy-on-write, so passing a large array costs nothing unless the function modifies it. Local functions defined at the end of a script are supported from R2016b. The file name must match the main function name for the function to be callable by that name.

tools.name: return
tools.description: Exits the current function immediately and returns control to the caller, using whatever values the output variables currently hold. Use it for early exits after a guard clause or when the answer is known before the rest of the body runs. In a script it stops execution of that script.
tools.usage: return
tools.notes: Unassigned output variables cause an error at the caller only if the caller actually requests them, so early returns must still assign every output that might be requested. `return` does not accept a value, unlike many other languages.

tools.name: nargin
tools.description: Returns the number of input arguments actually passed to the currently executing function, or, given a function name, the number that function declares. Use it to implement optional arguments and defaults in functions that do not use an `arguments` block. It counts only the arguments supplied, not the declared ones.
tools.usage:
n = nargin
n = nargin(fname)
n = nargin(fhandle)

parameters.name: fname
parameters.description: Function name whose declared input count is returned; negative when the function takes varargin.

tools.notes: A negative result from nargin(fname) means the function accepts varargin, with the magnitude giving the number of fixed arguments plus one. An `arguments` block with default values is the modern, self-documenting alternative.

tools.name: nargout
tools.description: Returns the number of output arguments the caller requested, letting a function skip expensive computations that nobody asked for. Given a function name it reports how many outputs that function declares. Use it to make optional outputs cheap.
tools.usage:
n = nargout
n = nargout(fname)
n = nargout(fhandle)

parameters.name: fname
parameters.description: Function name whose declared output count is returned.

tools.notes: Calling a function with no semicolon and no assignment gives nargout of 0, but `ans` is still assigned from the first output. Inside an anonymous function nargout is not meaningful.

tools.name: varargin
tools.description: A cell array holding all input arguments beyond the explicitly named ones, declared as the last input in the function signature. Use it for functions that take a variable number of arguments or trailing name-value pairs. Expand it with `varargin{:}` to forward the arguments to another function.
tools.notes: varargin must be the last declared input. Forwarding with `varargin{:}` preserves the original argument list exactly, which makes it the standard pattern for wrapper functions. For structured option handling, pass varargin to an `inputParser`.

tools.name: varargout
tools.description: A cell array holding the outputs a function returns beyond the explicitly named ones, declared as the last output in the signature. Assign its elements in a loop to return a data-dependent number of outputs. Use `nargout` to decide how many to produce.
tools.notes: Assigning fewer elements than the caller requested raises an error about an undefined output. varargout must be the last declared output and can be combined with named outputs before it.

tools.name: arguments
tools.description: Declares an argument validation block at the start of a function, specifying each input's size, class, validation functions and default value in a compact, declarative way. MATLAB validates and converts arguments before the body runs and produces standard, informative error messages. Use it in all new code in place of manual `nargin` checks and `validateattributes` calls.
tools.usage:
arguments
    name (dims) class {validators} = default
end
arguments (Repeating)
    ...
end
arguments
    options.Name (1,1) double = 1
end

parameters.name: (dims)
parameters.description: Size specification such as (1,1), (:,1) or (3,3).

parameters.name: class
parameters.description: Required class; compatible inputs are converted automatically.

parameters.name: {validators}
parameters.description: Validation functions such as mustBePositive, mustBeMember, mustBeNumeric.

parameters.name: = default
parameters.description: Default value making the argument optional.

parameters.name: options.Name
parameters.description: Declares a name-value pair argument.

tools.notes: Available since R2019b. The block must be the first executable code in the function, before any other statements. Size specifications also reshape compatible inputs, so declaring (:,1) turns a row vector input into a column automatically.

tools.name: inputParser
tools.description: An object that parses and validates function inputs, supporting required arguments, optional positional arguments, name-value pairs and parameter defaults. Results appear in its Results structure after calling parse. It predates the `arguments` block and is still useful when validation logic must be built dynamically.
tools.usage:
p = inputParser;
addRequired(p, name, validator)
addOptional(p, name, default, validator)
addParameter(p, name, default, validator)
parse(p, varargin{:})
p.Results.name

parameters.name: 'KeepUnmatched'
parameters.description: true to collect unrecognized names in p.Unmatched instead of erroring.

parameters.name: 'CaseSensitive'
parameters.description: Whether parameter names are matched case sensitively.

parameters.name: 'PartialMatching'
parameters.description: Allow abbreviated parameter names; true by default.

parameters.name: 'StructExpand'
parameters.description: Expand a struct argument into name-value pairs.

tools.notes: Setting FunctionName makes error messages name your function rather than the parser. For most new code the `arguments` block is faster, clearer and produces better error messages.

tools.name: validateattributes
tools.description: Checks that an input has the required classes and attributes such as size, sign, finiteness and monotonicity, throwing a descriptive error if not. Use it at the top of functions that must fail fast on bad input when an `arguments` block is not available. Supplying the function name and argument position produces clearer messages.
tools.usage:
validateattributes(A, classes, attributes)
validateattributes(A, classes, attributes, funcName, varName, argIndex)

parameters.name: classes
parameters.description: Cell array of allowed classes, for example {'numeric','logical'}.

parameters.name: attributes
parameters.description: Cell array such as {'nonempty','positive','integer','2d','size',[3 3],'>=',0}.

parameters.name: funcName, varName, argIndex
parameters.description: Context used in the error message.

tools.notes: Attributes are checked in order and the first failure throws, so put the cheapest checks first. The equivalent `mustBe*` validators inside an `arguments` block are more concise and are the recommended modern form.

tools.name: validatestring
tools.description: Matches a text input against a list of valid options, allowing case-insensitive and partial matches, and returns the full canonical option. It throws a helpful error listing the valid choices when nothing matches. Use it for string-valued options in functions that accept abbreviations.
tools.usage:
matchedStr = validatestring(str, validStrings)
matchedStr = validatestring(str, validStrings, funcName, varName, argIndex)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: Text to validate.

parameters.name: validStrings
parameters.description: Cell array or string array of acceptable values.

parameters.name: funcName, varName, argIndex
parameters.description: Context for the error message.

tools.example:
opts = {'linear','nearest','spline','pchip'};
validatestring('spl', opts)
validatestring('NEAREST', opts)
try
    validatestring('cubic2', opts, 'myfun', 'method', 2);
catch ME
    disp(ME.message)
end
tools.notes: Partial matching is convenient but ambiguous prefixes raise an error, so avoid option lists sharing long prefixes. Inside an `arguments` block, `mustBeMember` enforces exact membership instead.

tools.name: narginchk
tools.description: Verifies that the number of input arguments falls within a permitted range, throwing a standard error if not. Use it as a one-line guard at the top of functions with a variable number of inputs. `nargoutchk` performs the same check for outputs.
tools.usage:
narginchk(minArgs, maxArgs)
nargoutchk(minArgs, maxArgs)

parameters.name: minArgs
parameters.description: Minimum number of inputs required.

parameters.name: maxArgs
parameters.description: Maximum number allowed; use Inf for unlimited.

tools.notes: The error identifiers are MATLAB:narginchk:notEnoughInputs and MATLAB:narginchk:tooManyInputs, which callers can catch specifically. An `arguments` block enforces argument counts automatically.

tools.name: if
tools.description: Executes a block of statements when a condition is true, with optional elseif and else branches. The condition must reduce to a scalar logical, and an array condition is true only when every element is nonzero. Use short-circuit && and || in conditions so that guards evaluate safely.
tools.usage:
if expression
    statements
elseif expression
    statements
else
    statements
end

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: Condition; an array is true only if all its elements are nonzero, and an empty array is false.

tools.notes: `if v` on a vector means `if all(v)`, which silently hides bugs; be explicit with `any` or `all`. An empty condition is false, so `if []` never runs its body.

tools.name: switch
tools.description: Selects one of several blocks by comparing an expression against case values, with no fall-through between cases. A case may list several alternatives in a cell array, and `otherwise` handles everything else. Use it for dispatching on option strings and enumerations, where it reads better than a chain of elseif branches.
tools.usage:
switch expression
    case value
        statements
    case {v1, v2}
        statements
    otherwise
        statements
end

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: Scalar number, character vector, string scalar or enumeration to match.

parameters.name: case value
parameters.description: Value or cell array of values to compare against.

tools.notes: MATLAB never falls through to the next case, so no break statements are needed. Comparison uses `strcmp` for text and `==` for numbers, so a switch on a non-scalar numeric value never matches.

tools.name: for
tools.description: Repeats a block once for each column of the loop array, assigning that column to the loop variable. Iterating over a row vector therefore gives scalars, which is the usual case. Use it when an operation genuinely cannot be vectorized, and preallocate any array you fill inside the loop.
tools.usage:
for index = values
    statements
end
for index = 1:n
for c = cellArray
for col = matrix

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: Array, cell array or range; the loop runs once per column.

tools.notes: Modifying the loop variable inside the body does not affect the iteration sequence. Growing an array inside a loop without preallocation is the single most common MATLAB performance mistake. `parfor` runs independent iterations in parallel with Parallel Computing Toolbox.

tools.name: while
tools.description: Repeats a block as long as a condition remains true, testing before each iteration. Use it when the number of iterations is not known in advance, such as in iterative solvers and convergence loops. Always include a maximum iteration guard so a failure to converge cannot hang the program.
tools.usage:
while expression
    statements
end

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: Condition evaluated before each pass; an array is true only if all elements are nonzero.

tools.notes: A `while true` loop with an explicit break is often clearer than cramming a compound condition into the header. Press Ctrl+C to interrupt an accidental infinite loop.

tools.name: break
tools.description: Terminates the innermost enclosing for or while loop immediately and continues after its end. Use it to stop early once a result is found or a convergence criterion is met. It affects only one loop level, so nested loops need a flag or a function with `return` to exit both.
tools.usage: break
tools.notes: `break` is not allowed inside `parfor` because iterations are independent. To leave several nested loops at once, wrap them in a function and use `return`.

tools.name: continue
tools.description: Skips the rest of the current loop iteration and proceeds to the next one. Use it to filter out cases early and avoid deeply nested if blocks inside loops. Like `break`, it applies only to the innermost loop.
tools.usage: continue
tools.example:
total = 0;
for k = 1:20
    if mod(k, 3) ~= 0
        continue
    end
    total = total + k;
end
total
sum(3:3:20)
tools.notes: A `continue` early in the body is often more readable than wrapping the whole body in an if. In a `while` loop, make sure the loop variable still advances before the continue, or the loop will never end.

tools.name: try
tools.description: Runs a block of statements and transfers control to a catch block if an error occurs, optionally capturing the MException object that describes it. Use it to handle recoverable failures, to add context to errors, and to guarantee cleanup. Keep try blocks small so that unrelated errors are not swallowed.
tools.usage:
try
    statements
catch ME
    statements
end

parameters.name: ME
parameters.description: MException object with identifier, message, stack and cause fields.

tools.notes: Catching every error and continuing hides real bugs; always check the identifier and `rethrow` anything you did not expect. Ctrl+C interrupts are not catchable, and `onCleanup` is the reliable way to run cleanup code on any exit path.

tools.name: error
tools.description: Throws an error, stopping execution and returning control to the command prompt or the nearest catch block. Supplying an identifier of the form 'component:mnemonic' lets callers catch specific errors, and the message accepts sprintf-style formatting. Use it for conditions the function cannot handle.
tools.usage:
error(msg)
error(msg, A1, ..., An)
error(errID, msg, A1, ..., An)
error(errorStruct)
error(ME)

parameters.name: errID
parameters.description: Identifier such as 'myPkg:myFun:badInput', used for selective catching.

parameters.name: msg
parameters.description: Message text, with sprintf conversion specifications.

parameters.name: ME
parameters.description: An existing MException object to throw.

tools.notes: Always provide an identifier so callers can catch your errors specifically rather than by matching message text. A message containing a literal percent sign or backslash must be escaped, or passed through the single-argument form with no formatting.

tools.name: warning
tools.description: Issues a warning message without stopping execution, and also controls which warnings are displayed. With an identifier, individual warnings can be turned off and back on, and the previous state can be saved and restored. Use warnings for recoverable problems the user should know about.
tools.usage:
warning(msg)
warning(msg, A1, ..., An)
warning(warnID, msg, ...)
warning('off', warnID)
warning('on', warnID)
s = warning('query', warnID)
warning(s)

parameters.name: warnID
parameters.description: Warning identifier.

parameters.name: 'off'/'on'/'query'
parameters.description: Control or query the state of a warning.

parameters.name: 'error'
parameters.description: Promote the named warning to an error.

tools.notes: Saving the state returned by `warning('off', id)` and restoring it afterwards prevents your function from permanently changing the user's settings. Promoting a warning to an error with `warning('error', id)` is a good debugging technique for tracking down where it originates.

tools.name: MException
tools.description: Constructs an exception object carrying an identifier, a formatted message, a stack trace and optional causes, which can be thrown later or inspected in a catch block. Use it when you need to build an error before deciding to throw it, to attach causes, or to accumulate several failures. `throw`, `throwAsCaller` and `rethrow` all take an MException.
tools.usage:
ME = MException(errID, msg, A1, ..., An)
throw(ME)
throwAsCaller(ME)
ME = addCause(ME, causeME)
report = getReport(ME)

parameters.name: errID
parameters.description: Error identifier.

parameters.name: msg
parameters.description: Message text with optional sprintf formatting.

parameters.name: ME.identifier, ME.message, ME.stack, ME.cause
parameters.description: Properties of the exception.

tools.notes: `throwAsCaller` hides your function from the reported stack, which makes validation errors point at the caller's line. `getReport` produces the formatted text MATLAB would have displayed, useful for logging.

tools.name: rethrow
tools.description: Rethrows a previously caught exception, preserving its original identifier, message and stack. Use it in a catch block after handling only the cases you recognize, so that unexpected errors propagate unchanged. It is the correct way to avoid swallowing errors.
tools.usage: rethrow(ME)

parameters.name: ME
parameters.description: MException object caught earlier.

tools.notes: `rethrow` keeps the original stack, while `error(ME)` and `throw(ME)` reset it to the current location. Use `MException.addCause` first if you want to wrap the original error in a more descriptive one.

tools.name: assert
tools.description: Throws an error when a condition is false, with an optional identifier and formatted message. Use it to state invariants and preconditions that should never fail if the code is correct, and in tests. Unlike some languages, MATLAB assertions are always active and cannot be disabled.
tools.usage:
assert(cond)
assert(cond, msg)
assert(cond, msg, A1, ..., An)
assert(cond, errID, msg, ...)

parameters.name: cond
parameters.description: Condition that must be true.

parameters.name: errID
parameters.description: Error identifier.

parameters.name: msg
parameters.description: Message with sprintf formatting.

tools.notes: Because assertions always run, avoid expensive checks in hot loops. For user-facing input validation prefer an `arguments` block or `validateattributes`, which give better messages; reserve assert for internal invariants.

tools.name: onCleanup
tools.description: Creates an object that runs a specified function when it is destroyed, which happens when the enclosing function exits for any reason, including an error or Ctrl+C. Use it to guarantee that files are closed, paths restored, figures deleted and settings reverted. It is more reliable than putting cleanup code in a catch block.
tools.usage: c = onCleanup(@() cleanupFunction)

parameters.description: Function handle taking no arguments, executed when the object is cleared.

tools.notes: The object must be assigned to a variable, or it is destroyed immediately and the cleanup runs at once. Cleanup objects created in a script run only when the variable is cleared, so this pattern belongs in functions.

tools.name: function_handle
tools.description: The @ operator creates a function handle, either a reference to a named function or an anonymous function with a body and captured workspace variables. Handles let functions be stored in variables, passed as arguments and built at run time. Anonymous functions capture the values of outer variables at creation time, not at call time.
tools.usage:
h = @functionName
h = @(arg1, arg2) expression
h(args)

parameters.name: @name
parameters.description: Handle to an existing function.

parameters.name: @(args) expr
parameters.description: Anonymous function; expr must be a single expression.

tools.notes: Because anonymous functions freeze their captured variables, updating a captured variable later has no effect; recreate the handle instead. Anonymous functions are limited to a single expression, so use a local function for anything longer.

tools.name: feval
tools.description: Calls a function specified by a handle or by name, passing the given arguments and returning its outputs. Use it when the function to call is decided at run time, for example from a configuration string. With a handle, calling it directly is faster and clearer than feval.
tools.usage:
feval(fun, x1, ..., xn)
[y1, ..., ym] = feval(___)

parameters.name: fun
parameters.description: Function handle, or function name as a character vector.

parameters.name: x1,...,xn
parameters.description: Arguments to pass.

tools.notes: Calling by name is slower because MATLAB must resolve the name each time; convert once with `str2func` when calling repeatedly. feval on a name from untrusted input executes arbitrary code.

tools.name: func2str
tools.description: Converts a function handle to a character vector containing its text, including the body of an anonymous function. Use it for logging which function was used, for display in reports, and for saving configurations in human-readable form. The text of an anonymous function does not include the values it captured.
tools.usage: chr = func2str(fh)

parameters.name: fh
parameters.description: Function handle.

tools.notes: The captured workspace is lost in the string form, so recreating the handle with `str2func` in a different context gives a different function. `functions(fh)` returns a struct describing the handle, including its captured variables.

tools.name: str2func
tools.description: Creates a function handle from text, either a function name or the text of an anonymous function. Use it to build callables from configuration files and user input, and to speed up repeated calls that would otherwise go through `feval` by name. Handles created this way have no captured workspace.
tools.usage: fh = str2func(str)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: Function name, or anonymous function text such as '@(x) x.^2'.

tools.notes: Creating a handle from an anonymous function string evaluates arbitrary code, so never build one from untrusted input. A handle to a name that does not exist is created successfully but fails when called.

tools.name: cellfun
tools.description: Applies a function to every element of one or more cell arrays. By default it expects scalar outputs and returns an array; set UniformOutput to false to collect arbitrary results in a cell array. Use it to process lists of heterogeneous items without an explicit loop.
tools.usage:
A = cellfun(func, C)
A = cellfun(func, C1, ..., Cn)
C = cellfun(func, C, 'UniformOutput', false)
[A, B] = cellfun(___)
A = cellfun(func, C, 'ErrorHandler', ehandle)

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Function handle applied to each element, or one of a few built-in names such as 'isempty' and 'length'.

parameters.name: 'UniformOutput'
parameters.description: true (default) requires scalar outputs; false returns a cell array.

parameters.name: 'ErrorHandler'
parameters.description: Function called when func errors on an element.

tools.notes: cellfun is not faster than a preallocated for loop; it is chosen for clarity, not speed. Forgetting 'UniformOutput', false when the function returns non-scalars is the usual error.

tools.name: arrayfun
tools.description: Applies a function to each element of one or more arrays, returning an array of scalar results or, with UniformOutput false, a cell array. Use it when a computation cannot be vectorized and must be done element by element, such as calling a solver for each parameter value. For genuinely vectorizable operations, direct array arithmetic is far faster.
tools.usage:
B = arrayfun(func, A)
B = arrayfun(func, A1, ..., An)
C = arrayfun(func, A, 'UniformOutput', false)
[B, D] = arrayfun(___)

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Function handle called once per element.

parameters.name: 'UniformOutput'
parameters.description: true (default) or false.

parameters.name: 'ErrorHandler'
parameters.description: Handler invoked when func errors.

tools.notes: `arrayfun(@(k) k^2, 1:5)` is many times slower than `(1:5).^2`; reach for it only when the body truly needs scalars. It also works over struct arrays, calling the function once per element.

tools.name: structfun
tools.description: Applies a function to the value of every field of a scalar structure, returning a column vector of scalar results or a structure when UniformOutput is false. Use it to validate, transform or summarize all fields of a configuration or results struct at once. The function receives field values, not names.
tools.usage:
A = structfun(func, S)
S2 = structfun(func, S, 'UniformOutput', false)
[A, B] = structfun(___)

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Function handle applied to each field value.

parameters.name: 'UniformOutput'
parameters.description: true (default) returns a vector; false returns a struct.

parameters.name: 'ErrorHandler'
parameters.description: Handler invoked on error.

tools.notes: structfun requires a scalar struct; use `arrayfun` over a struct array. To work with field names as well as values, loop over `fieldnames(s)` with dynamic field access.

tools.name: deal
tools.description: Distributes its inputs to its outputs, either one-to-one or by copying a single input to every output. Use it to assign several variables at once, to unpack a comma-separated list from a cell array or struct array, and inside anonymous functions that must return several values. It is the canonical way to set many struct array fields to the same value.
tools.usage:
[a, b, c] = deal(x)
[a, b, c] = deal(x, y, z)
[s.field] = deal(value)

parameters.name: x, y, z
parameters.description: Values to distribute; one input is copied to all outputs.

tools.notes: `[s.field] = deal(v)` is the idiom for setting a field across a whole struct array. In an anonymous function, `@(x) deal(x+1, x-1)` allows two outputs, which a plain expression cannot provide.

tools.name: global
tools.description: Declares a variable as global so that it is shared by every function and workspace that declares it with the same name. Use it sparingly, for genuinely session-wide settings, because globals make data flow hard to follow and break reuse. Passing arguments, using nested functions or persistent state is almost always preferable.
tools.usage:
global var1 var2
clear global var1

parameters.name: var1
parameters.description: Name of the variable to share; it must be declared global in every workspace that uses it.

tools.notes: A global that has not been assigned is an empty array in every workspace, so always check with `isempty`. `clear global name` removes it everywhere, and `clear` alone does not.

tools.name: persistent
tools.description: Declares variables inside a function that keep their values between calls but remain private to that function. Use them for caches, call counters, lazily initialized tables and simple state machines. They are initialized to empty, which gives a natural first-call test.
tools.usage:
persistent var1 var2
clear functionName

parameters.name: var1
parameters.description: Name of the persistent variable.

tools.notes: `clear functionName` resets a function's persistent variables, which is essential when testing. Editing the file also clears them, which can make behaviour during development look inconsistent.

tools.name: eval
tools.description: Executes a character vector as MATLAB code in the current workspace. It defeats the code analyser, prevents JIT optimization and is a security risk with untrusted input, so it should be avoided in almost all cases. Dynamic field names, function handles, containers and cell arrays cover nearly every legitimate use.
tools.usage:
eval(expression)
eval(expression, catchExpression)
output = eval(expression)

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: Text containing MATLAB statements.

parameters.name: catchExpression
parameters.description: Text evaluated if the first expression errors.

tools.example:
eval('x = 5;')
x
v = eval('1 + 2')
% avoid this pattern:
% for k = 1:3, eval(sprintf('a%d = k;', k)); end
% use this instead:
a = cell(1, 3);
for k = 1:3, a{k} = k; end
tools.notes: Creating numbered variables with eval is the classic anti-pattern; use arrays, cell arrays, structs or `dictionary` instead. Code containing eval cannot be compiled by MATLAB Coder and runs much more slowly.

tools.name: evalin
tools.description: Evaluates an expression in the 'base' or 'caller' workspace rather than the current one. It is used mainly by GUIs, debugging tools and legacy code that must reach into another scope. As with `eval`, prefer explicit argument passing in ordinary code.
tools.usage:
evalin(ws, expression)
evalin(ws, expression, catchExpression)
output = evalin(___)

parameters.name: ws
parameters.description: 'base' or 'caller'.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: Code to evaluate in that workspace.

tools.notes: Reaching into the caller's workspace couples functions to their callers and breaks when variables are renamed. `assignin` is the counterpart that writes rather than reads.

tools.name: assignin
tools.description: Assigns a value to a variable in the 'base' or 'caller' workspace. It is used by interactive tools that need to place results where the user can see them, such as import dialogs and app callbacks. Ordinary functions should return values instead.
tools.usage: assignin(ws, varname, value)

parameters.name: ws
parameters.description: 'base' or 'caller'.

parameters.name: varname
parameters.description: Name of the variable to create or overwrite.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Value to assign.

tools.notes: assignin silently overwrites an existing variable of that name. Returning the value and letting the caller decide where to put it is better practice for library code.

tools.name: exist
tools.description: Reports whether a name exists as a variable, file, folder, function, class or Java class, returning a numeric code that identifies the kind. Use it to test for optional files and to check whether a function is available before calling it. Always pass the second argument to restrict the search, since a bare call checks many categories.
tools.usage:
tf = exist(name)
tf = exist(name, searchType)

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Name to look up.

parameters.name: searchType
parameters.description: 'var', 'file', 'dir', 'builtin', 'class'.

tools.example:
x = 1;
exist('x', 'var')
exist('sin', 'builtin')
exist('data.csv', 'file')
exist('results', 'dir')
if ~exist('outdir', 'dir'), mkdir('outdir'); end
tools.notes: The return codes are 0 none, 1 variable, 2 file, 3 MEX, 4 Simulink model, 5 built-in, 6 P-file, 7 folder, 8 class. Without the second argument, a variable named `sin` would shadow the function in the result, so always specify the type.

tools.name: isvarname
tools.description: Tests whether a piece of text is a valid MATLAB variable name: letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, within the maximum name length, and not a reserved keyword. Use it before creating dynamic field names or variable names from external data. `matlab.lang.makeValidName` converts invalid text into a valid name.
tools.usage: tf = isvarname(str)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: Text to test.

tools.example:
isvarname('myVar')
isvarname('2ndValue')
isvarname('my var')
isvarname('end')
matlab.lang.makeValidName({'2nd Value', 'my var'})
matlab.lang.makeUniqueStrings({'a','a','b'})
tools.notes: Table variable names and struct field names must be valid variable names for dot access to work, although tables can store other names accessed with `T.('odd name')`. `namelengthmax` gives the maximum allowed length.

tools.name: mfilename
tools.description: Returns the name of the currently executing file, and with the 'fullpath' option its full path without the extension. Use it in error messages, in logging, and to locate data files stored alongside the code. Called from the command line it returns an empty character vector.
tools.usage:
name = mfilename
fullPath = mfilename('fullpath')
className = mfilename('class')

parameters.name: 'fullpath'
parameters.description: Return the full path without the file extension.

parameters.name: 'class'
parameters.description: Return the class name when called from a class method.

tools.notes: `fileparts(mfilename('fullpath'))` is the standard way to find a function's own folder so that bundled data files can be located regardless of the current directory. Inside an anonymous function it reports the enclosing file.
